title: The short books, closed
hookLine: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka
last: AS HE SPEAKS, SO HE DOES.

lines: A VERSE KEPT IN A WALLET.
cards: Some of the best things people say are short. A grandparent's one line at a wedding. A note left on the fridge.
A verse someone copied onto a card and kept in a wallet for years.
These last weeks lived in books like that: not the long discourses, with their journeys and debates, but three small collections of verses and sayings, some of them only a few lines long.
They're shelved together in the Pali canon's Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short texts.

teach.b: First, the Sutta Nipata, which some scholars count among the earliest Buddhist poetry. It opened with a monk shedding the world like a snake sheds its skin. Walking alone like the rhinoceros horn, or with a good friend.

The discourse on kindness again, the jewel discourse, and the highest blessings, from caring for parents to a mind unshaken. A boat, the dart of grief, the chapter of eights, and the long road to the far shore.
Second, the Udana, inspired sayings, words the Buddha spoke when something moved him. In the seen, only the seen. Boys tormenting fish.
The blind men each holding a part of the elephant. And the rare, quiet line: because there is, an escape is known.

teach.h: THE ITIVUTTAKA: THUS IT WAS SAID
teach.b: Third, the Itivuttaka, thus it was said, sayings remembered, the tradition says, by a woman who heard them and repeated them for others. Share even the last bite. Two bright guardians, conscience and concern.
The whirlpool ahead. Parents as first teachers. Effort is alive.
And word and deed made one. What do the three books share? They're compact; a whole teaching fits in a breath or two.
They're made to be memorized and chanted, and some still are.

teach.h: SHORT SAYINGS ASK MORE OF YOU
teach.b: And they're not shallow for being short. A long discourse explains itself.
A short verse leaves room, and you have to step into it. Tomorrow a very different kind of book begins, thousands of discourses sorted by subject.

how: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, such as the discourse on kindness, the jewel discourse and the highest blessings, are among the texts Theravada communities chant regularly, and some Buddhists learn short sayings from these books by heart.

small, short, as in short texts

games.q: you've spent weeks in the short books, and you can keep just one line. what do these books ask of you?
o: pick one short line and step into it.
skip ahead to the longer books.
games.why: a short verse leaves room. the books were made to be carried in a breath, and lived with.

practice: Let these last weeks drift past: the snake's skin, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the boat, the elephant, the whirlpool, the first teachers.
Don't try to remember them all; wait for one to stay, and whichever comes back on its own, say its line quietly to yourself, as short as you can make it. Breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Khuddaka, small or short. The Sutta Nipata, the Udana and the Itivuttaka, three small collections of verse and saying from the Khuddaka Nikaya: short, and deep. Today's word.
